_comment: What this was last verified against, and the reason the file exists.
The kernel module in contrib/npuep is C against one kernel's headers. When OPNsense ships a
new kernel the installed module is no longer the right one - and because the boot hook is
written to exit 0 rather than block a boot, the appliance comes up quietly with no front
ports. The silence is deliberate and it is also how this would go unnoticed.
WHAT TO COMPARE, AND WHAT NOT TO. The first two fields below are labels. They are what a
human reads and they are NOT what breaks: OPNsense ships kernel sets inside a series, so
26.7 -> 26.7.4 changes /boot/kernel while leaving 'OPNsense 26.7' and 'FreeBSD
15.1-RELEASE-p1' both untouched. That happened here, and the labels did not move an inch.
kern_version is the field to compare, because it carries the source commit the kernel was
built from and nothing else in the system does.
upstream_release is a third thing again - the newest opnsense/core RELEASE TAG that has
been verified here. .github/workflows/upstream.yml compares it against the tag list in
full rather than on major.minor, because a point release is exactly the case that ships
a kernel while leaving the labels alone.
Nor does a mismatch announce itself at load time. A module declares its kernel dependency as
a RANGE - from the __FreeBSD_version it was built against to the end of that branch - so a
module built for 15.1 loads without complaint into any later 15.x kernel. The loud refusal
this project once expected does not arrive; the module loads and reads any structure that
moved at the wrong offset. contrib/npuep/build.sh therefore stamps the module with the
kernel it was built against, and install/verify.sh compares the stamp rather than probing.
So: .github/workflows/upstream.yml watches for a new OPNsense release and raises an issue,
and install/verify.sh is what to run on the ARMADA appliance afterwards. It knows nothing
about octep, so the OCTEON TX entry is updated from the hand-run bring-up instead. Update a
board's fields only after that board's own check has passed on real hardware.
WHY boards IS A LIST. This began as one appliance and the file described it in the singular.
There are two now, and they are not the same silicon - an ARMADA CN9131 and a Cavium OCTEON TX
CN83XX - so 'board' could no longer be one string. The kernel fields above stay at the top
level on purpose: both appliances run the same OPNsense kernel from the same source commit, so
those are facts about the build and not about a board. Only what differs per board moved down.
Each entry says what was verified and how. 'works' is deliberately narrow: it is what has been
seen carrying traffic on that board, not what the driver is meant to do. A board whose front
ports have never been driven says so.

boards.works: all 14 front ports carry traffic in both directions as ordinary FreeBSD interfaces
boards.verified_how: install/verify.sh on the appliance, after a cold boot, with the driver loaded by the boot hook

boards.works: the management link pings across PCIe at 0 percent loss; the endpoint handshake completes; a front port is raised over NetAgent and its link read back; a 10G link on a front cage trains; the RPC facility is configured and PPORT_UPDATE and LIF_ADD_UPDATE are accepted; and frames posted on an SDP ring are transmitted on a front port, come back on another, and are written into host memory, where one was read out byte for byte - the fast path's own named counters account for every frame in both directions with every drop counter at zero. What still fails is the rate: each armed ring delivers one packet and then stops, so there is no usable interface yet.
boards.verified_how: driver loaded by hand; link state read back through NetAgent attribute 0x00 and confirmed by disabling one end and watching the other follow; the RPC facility configured and its platform block read back and checked field for field against the vendor firmware's own capture; traffic confirmed on a front port by reading the fast path's own 182 named counters around a controlled fifty-frame burst, where RX_KN, FROM_KN_TO_WIRE, TX_WIRE, RX_WIRE, FROM_WIRE_TO_KN_LIF_OFFLOAD_DISABLED and TX_KN each rose by exactly fifty. An earlier egress claim that rested on the SFP cage LEDs stays withdrawn, because those cages have no LED key; this is a different instrument. The return direction was confirmed by reading the receive buffer out of physical memory and decoding the 82-byte prefix and the frame behind it, and the one-packet-per-ring limit by driving the link from a second machine so that frames spread across all eight rings instead of hashing to one

version_sensitive: contrib/npuep/*.c - rebuild required on any kernel change, which means any change to kern_version and not merely to the two labels above

contrib/octep/*.c - the same, for the OCTEON TX driver. build.sh stamps octep.ko.kernel with uname -v and a mismatch is silent, because a module built against a different 15.x kernel loads without complaint
src/etc/rc.syshook.d/early/* - depends on OPNsense running early syshooks before it configures interfaces, and on being numbered after OPNsense's own 05-upgrade
